# ai-memory

One shared memory for all my AI tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Muse, ...).
A skill created in any tool lives here, and every other tool can read and use it.

## Layout

```
skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md   # one folder per skill (plus optional scripts/, references/)
artifacts/                     # reusable outputs: templates, docs, snippets
prompts/                       # standalone prompts worth keeping
templates/SKILL.template.md    # copy this when adding a skill by hand
server/                        # MCP server (coming next)
```

## SKILL.md format

Every skill starts with YAML frontmatter so the MCP server can list and search it:

```yaml
---
name: meeting-notes            # kebab-case, same as folder name
description: One line on what it does and when to use it
source: chatgpt                # where it was created: claude | chatgpt | codex | muse | other
tags: [writing, work]
---
```

## Adding a skill

1. Copy `templates/SKILL.template.md` to `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
2. Fill in the frontmatter and paste the instructions.
3. `git add . && git commit -m "Add <name> skill" && git push`

On another device: `git pull` and the skill is there.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\971367\AppData\Roaming\Claude\local-agent-mode-sessions\skills-plugin\d0eaddda-89b6-4146-8a96-6ca8e8e440e7\0d7e9b11-cac0-4d59-a309-f0c22c1d19e1\skills\frontend-design

This skill guides creation of distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces that avoid generic "AI slop" aesthetics. Implement real working code with exceptional attention to aesthetic details and creative choices.

The user provides frontend requirements: a component, page, application, or interface to build. They may include context about the purpose, audience, or technical constraints.

## Design Thinking

Before coding, understand the context and commit to a BOLD aesthetic direction:
- **Purpose**: What problem does this interface solve? Who uses it?
- **Tone**: Pick an extreme: brutally minimal, maximalist chaos, retro-futuristic, organic/natural, luxury/refined, playful/toy-like, editorial/magazine, brutalist/raw, art deco/geometric, soft/pastel, industrial/utilitarian, etc. There are so many flavors to choose from. Use these for inspiration but design one that is true to the aesthetic direction.
- **Constraints**: Technical requirements (framework, performance, accessibility).
- **Differentiation**: What makes this UNFORGETTABLE? What's the one thing someone will remember?

**CRITICAL**: Choose a clear conceptual direction and execute it with precision. Bold maximalism and refined minimalism both work - the key is intentionality, not intensity.

Then implement working code (HTML/CSS/JS, React, Vue, etc.) that is:
- Production-grade and functional
- Visually striking and memorable
- Cohesive with a clear aesthetic point-of-view
- Meticulously refined in every detail

## Frontend Aesthetics Guidelines

Focus on:
- **Typography**: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices that elevate the frontend's aesthetics; unexpected, characterful font choices. Pair a distinctive display font with a refined body font.
- **Color & Theme**: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency. Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes.
- **Motion**: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only solutions for HTML. Use Motion library for React when available. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered micro-interactions. Use scroll-triggering and hover states that surprise.
- **Spatial Composition**: Unexpected layouts. Asymmetry. Overlap. Diagonal flow. Grid-breaking elements. Generous negative space OR controlled density.
- **Backgrounds & Visual Details**: Create atmosphere and depth rather than defaulting to solid colors. Add contextual effects and textures that match the overall aesthetic. Apply creative forms like gradient meshes, noise textures, geometric patterns, layered transparencies, dramatic shadows, decorative borders, custom cursors, and grain overlays.

NEVER use generic AI-generated aesthetics like overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts), cliched color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds), predictable layouts and component patterns, and cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character.

Interpret creatively and make unexpected choices that feel genuinely designed for the context. No design should be the same. Vary between light and dark themes, different fonts, different aesthetics. NEVER converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations.

**IMPORTANT**: Match implementation complexity to the aesthetic vision. Maximalist designs need elaborate code with extensive animations and effects. Minimalist or refined designs need restraint, precision, and careful attention to spacing, typography, and subtle details. Elegance comes from executing the vision well.

Remember: Claude is capable of extraordinary creative work. Don't hold back, show what can truly be created when thinking outside the box and committing fully to a distinctive vision.

# Deploys the site to Google Cloud Run with Firestore storage.
# Usage:  .\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId my-gcp-project [-Region us-central1] [-Service groundwork-site]
# Prereqs: gcloud CLI installed and `gcloud auth login` done; billing enabled on the project.
param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$ProjectId,
  [string]$Region = "us-central1",
  [string]$Service = "groundwork-site",
  [string]$FirestoreLocation = "nam5"
)
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$sa = "$Service-sa@$ProjectId.iam.gserviceaccount.com"

Write-Host "==> Using project $ProjectId"
gcloud config set project $ProjectId

Write-Host "==> Enabling APIs"
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com firestore.googleapis.com

Write-Host "==> Ensuring Firestore (default) database exists"
$dbs = gcloud firestore databases list --format="value(name)" 2>$null
if (-not ($dbs -match "/databases/\(default\)")) {
  gcloud firestore databases create --location=$FirestoreLocation --type=firestore-native
}

Write-Host "==> Ensuring service account $sa"
$existing = gcloud iam service-accounts list --filter="email:$sa" --format="value(email)"
if (-not $existing) {
  gcloud iam service-accounts create "$Service-sa" --display-name="$Service runtime"
}
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $ProjectId --member="serviceAccount:$sa" --role="roles/datastore.user" --condition=None | Out-Null

Write-Host "==> Building and deploying to Cloud Run"
gcloud run deploy $Service `
  --source . `
  --region $Region `
  --service-account $sa `
  --allow-unauthenticated `
  --set-env-vars "STORAGE=firestore,FIRESTORE_COLLECTION=bookings" `
  --memory 256Mi `
  --cpu 1 `
  --min-instances 0 `
  --max-instances 3 `
  --concurrency 80 `
  --timeout 30

Write-Host "==> Done. URL:"
gcloud run services describe $Service --region $Region --format="value(status.url)"

# Groundwork AI: website + booking backend

Marketing site and booking form for a hands-on AI setup service aimed at project managers and leaders in
mechanical, electrical, aviation and marine. Built to run on **Google Cloud Run**, with bookings stored in
**Firestore** (free tier).

## What's inside

```
public/            Static site (no build step)
  index.html       Home: hero, About us (click-to-play session animation), Services (live pipeline), Security, How to book
  book.html        Booking form: name, role, company, industry, email, phone, date/time/time zone, details
  styles.css       Theme ("engineering drawing": drafting paper, navy ink, safety orange)
  main.js          Nav, scroll reveals, animation controls
  book.js          Form validation + submit to /api/bookings
src/
  server.js        Entry point, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM
  app.js           Express app: security headers/CSP, rate limiting, API, static files
  validation.js    Server-side validation (zod)
  db.js            Storage: Firestore in production, in-memory for local dev
test/api.test.js   API tests (node:test)
Dockerfile         Production image (Node 22 alpine, non-root)
deploy.ps1         One-command Cloud Run + Firestore deploy
```

### Production features
- Strict Content-Security-Policy, HSTS and other headers (helmet). No inline scripts.
- Rate limiting on bookings (5 per 15 min per IP), 16 KB body limit, honeypot spam trap.
- Validation runs in the browser and again on the server.
- Structured JSON logs that show up properly in Cloud Logging.
- `/healthz` (liveness) and `/readyz` (checks Firestore) endpoints.
- Accessible: skip link, labelled fields, keyboard focus styles, `prefers-reduced-motion` support.

## Run locally

```bash
npm install
npm start          # http://localhost:8080 (bookings kept in memory)
npm test
```

## Deploy to Cloud Run

1. Install the [gcloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install), then run `gcloud auth login`.
2. Create a Google Cloud project and link a billing account. Cloud Run needs billing enabled, but a
   low-traffic site like this normally stays inside the free tiers.
3. From this folder, in PowerShell:

```powershell
.\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID
```

The script enables the APIs, creates the Firestore `(default)` database (the free tier only applies to that
one), creates a least-privilege service account (`roles/datastore.user`), then builds and deploys with
Cloud Build. You don't need Docker installed locally.

### Viewing bookings
Google Cloud Console → **Firestore** → `bookings` collection. Each document has the form fields plus
`status: "new"` and `createdAt`.

### Custom domain
Cloud Run → your service → **Manage custom domains**, or put it behind a global HTTPS load balancer.

## Before going live: replace placeholders
- Brand name **Groundwork AI** (HTML titles, header, footer).
- `hello@example.com` in `index.html` and `book.html`.
- Add a privacy policy page. You collect names, emails and phone numbers.

The website is built in a new folder, `C:\Users\971367\ai-service-site`, separate from your `ai-memory` repo. It runs locally at http://localhost:8080 and the 8 automated tests pass. I haven't deployed it to Cloud Run: `gcloud` isn't installed on this machine, and deploying needs your Google Cloud project.

## Your business idea

It's a good idea. "A real person sets up AI on your laptop and explains it in plain English" fills a real gap. Senior people in engineering fields don't have time to learn these tools, and they trust a person more than a product. A few things to sort out early:

1. **Company laptops.** Many clients will be on laptops their employer manages. Installing software or remoting in can break company policy. Expect to work with their IT team, or start with owner-run businesses and consultancies. I put a "we work within your IT policies" message on the site for this reason.
2. **Their data.** You'll see confidential project information. You'll want a simple contract, an NDA, and ideally professional liability insurance before your first paying client.
3. **Scaling.** One-to-one time doesn't scale. Fixed packages (for example "Claude + Outlook setup", "3 automations") plus a monthly support plan will help.
4. **Your day job.** If you're still employed full-time, check your employer's policy on outside work before you launch.

## What's built

- **Top menu:** About us · Services · How to book · Book a call.
- **About us:** explains that you're a real service-desk team, not a chatbot. It has a 7-second animation that plays when clicked: an engineer connects through a secure, client-approved tunnel to a laptop. A checklist then fills in (Claude installed → Outlook connected → Report scheduled) and an "Automated" badge appears. There's a Replay button.
- **Services:** eight services, including setting up Claude, connectors, custom skills, and workflows with Claude and Codex, plus an "any other setup" card. Beside them runs a looping animation of an example automation (a Monday 7 AM project digest).
- **Security section:** sessions run through tools like BeyondTrust, the client approves and watches everything, and no passwords are ever shared.
- **How to book:** four steps and a call-to-action.
- **Booking page** ([book.html](public/book.html)): name, role, company, industry, email, phone, preferred date and time, time zone (detected automatically), other availability, details, and a consent checkbox. After submitting, the visitor sees a confirmation with a reference number.
- **Database:** Firestore, Google's own database. Its free tier is generous and it works with Cloud Run without managing passwords or keys. You view bookings in the Firestore console.
- **Production basics:** security headers, spam protection and rate limiting on the form, checks in both the browser and the server, health-check endpoints, and a Docker image.

The look is styled like an engineering drawing: drafting-grid paper, navy ink and safety-orange accents, so it feels familiar to people in mechanical, aviation and marine work.

In the browser I checked:
- the desktop and mobile layouts
- the animation from start to finish
- empty-form error messages
- a complete test booking reaching the server

The preview pane couldn't screenshot sections lower down the page, so I hid the sections above them in the preview to look at each part.

## To deploy

1. Install the [gcloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install) and sign in with `gcloud auth login`.
2. Create a Google Cloud project and turn on billing. Cloud Run requires billing to be enabled, but a site with this little traffic normally stays within the free tiers.
3. Run this from the project folder:

```bash
.\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID
```

The script sets up the database and a restricted service account, then builds and deploys the site. You don't need Docker. The [README](README.md) covers this, plus viewing bookings and adding a custom domain.

## Before going live
- **"Groundwork AI"** is a placeholder name I made up. Replace it with your real business name.
- Replace `hello@example.com` with your contact email.
- Add a privacy policy page, since the form collects names, emails and phone numbers.
- New bookings don't notify you yet. You have to check Firestore. I can add an email alert when a booking comes in if you'd like.

I created a git repo in the folder but haven't committed anything. Tell me if you want me to commit it, or push it to GitHub.

content.text:
You were right that it didn't come across. The old animation sat behind a play button with no controls, so it didn't look like a video. It's now a proper video-style player in the **About us** section, and I tested every part in the browser.

**What it does:**
- **Plays on its own** when you scroll to it, loops every 10 seconds, and pauses when you scroll away.
- **Controls like a video:** play/pause, restart, a progress bar and a `0:04 / 0:10` time counter. Clicking the picture also pauses or plays it.
- **Four scenes with subtitles:**
  1. Speech bubbles: "What slows you down?" / "Weekly reports!"
  2. A secure, encrypted connection forms and data moves across it.
  3. A checklist fills in on the laptop: Claude installed, Outlook connected, Report scheduled.
  4. An "Automated" badge and a "Mon 7:00 · Report sent" notification appear.
- **Clickable steps:** the four steps under the picture jump straight to that scene.

**Other animations on the page:**
- **Top of the page:** tasks get crossed out with their new, shorter times.
- **Below that:** a scrolling band of industries.
- **Next to Services:** an example automation runs on a loop.
- **While scrolling:** sections fade in.

**Two fixes that may explain why you saw nothing:**
- **Opening the file directly:** if you double-clicked `index.html`, it loaded without its styles and scripts, so nothing moved. That's fixed. The booking form still needs the server to save requests.
- **Browser caching:** the server told browsers to keep scripts for an hour, so returning visitors could see an old version after an update. It now checks for a fresh copy on every load.

**To see it:** the server is running. Open http://localhost:8080 and press **Ctrl+F5** to clear the old cached files, then scroll to About us.

**Sorry about your Cloud Console tab:** while testing, I loaded the site over your Google Cloud Console "New Project" page in the browser pane. I sent that tab back to the Cloud Console page, but anything you'd typed into that form may have been lost. I did the rest of the testing in a separate tab.

If you want an actual recorded video, like a screen recording of a real setup session, save it as `public/assets/intro.mp4` and I'll swap it in.

Yes, the whole project is on your computer, in `C:\Users\971367\ai-service-site`. Nothing has been uploaded anywhere.

**What committing does:** it saves a snapshot of the project, like a save point. It stays on your computer only. The folder isn't linked to GitHub or any other online copy, so nothing gets published. Pushing to GitHub would be a separate step later.

**Where it stands now:** I set up git in the folder, but nothing has been committed yet. So right now there is no save point to go back to.

**Can you get today's version back after more changes?** Only if you commit first:
1. **Commit now** to save the current version as a save point.
2. Ask me for more changes.
3. If you don't like them, tell me "go back to the previous version" and I'll restore that save point, either the whole project or only certain files.

Without a commit first, undoing changes means rebuilding the old version by hand, which isn't guaranteed to be exact.

**About the "Commit changes" button:** I'm not certain which folder it uses. This session started in your `ai-memory` folder before moving to `ai-service-site`, so it could commit in the wrong one. It's safer to let me do it: I'll commit everything in `ai-service-site` with a short description. The installed libraries (`node_modules`) are left out on purpose, since they can be reinstalled with `npm install`.

content.text:
I made your text changes. Colours, layout and styling are unchanged, apart from the two things you asked me to fix: the letter shapes and the form.

**Wording**
- **About us:** now says you're forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) and experienced technical support engineers. The heading is now "Not a chatbot. *Real engineers* who deploy AI." I updated the top-of-page intro and the page description the same way.
- **01, AI tools:** now "Setting up your AI tools", covering Claude, ChatGPT & Codex, Grok, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot Studio and many more.
- **02, Connectors:** added Apollo, Figma, Firecrawl and external (MCP) servers.
- **03, Skills:** this card is gone. To keep the grid even, I replaced it with **Marketing & outreach** (contacts, campaigns, launches, LinkedIn/X posts). Skills are now mentioned inside Workflow automation instead.
- **04, Workflow automation:** reworded so it isn't about Claude or Codex, and the tags are now Claude · AI · App setup.
- **05, Scheduled jobs:** renamed **Scheduled automations**. It now covers job search, marketing emails, product launches, finding contacts, and the latest AI news delivered to your inbox.
- **Footer:** the Claude trademark line is replaced with "**You lead the work. We automate the rest.**"
- **About video:** I also changed "Claude installed" to "AI tools installed" and made one subtitle generic.

**Example automations:** there are now 6. Click the card and it moves to the next one, looping back after the last: daily site report, job search assistant, AI news briefing, Slack & email catch-up, LinkedIn & X updates, and the Monday project digest. A "1 / 6 · Click for next →" counter shows where you are.

**Letters bending:** two causes. The headings had very tight letter spacing, so letters like the f and l in "Workflow" ran into each other. The heading font also has quirky alternate shapes for some letters, which made them look like they lean. I loosened the spacing and turned the quirky shapes off. The font itself is the same.

**Booking form:** the time box only accepted 15-minute steps, so a time like 10:56 PM was quietly rejected and the form wouldn't send. That limit is gone. The time zone box is removed: it's detected automatically and shown under the date and time as "Times are in your local time zone: Pacific Daylight Time (America/Los_Angeles)." I tested a booking at 10:56 PM and it went through.

**Is "Groundwork AI" already taken?** Yes, by several companies. One is a [Brooklyn AI company](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/groundwork-ai) in geotechnical engineering, there's a [GroundWork AI technology consultancy](https://logo.com/brand/groundwork-ai), and another uses [groundworkai.com](https://www.kalibrr.com/id-ID/c/groundwork-ai/jobs). There are also similar names: ["GROUNDWORK" trademark filings](https://trademark.justia.com/category/computer-and-scientific/2024/november/20/3.html), and [GroundWork Technologies](https://trademarks.justia.com/owners/groundwork-technologies-llc-5265752). The consultancy is close to what you'd offer, so I'd rename before launch. The logo is a simple crosshair I drew from scratch, so it's low risk, but it should change with the name. Some ideas: **Forward Bench**, **Handover AI**, **Deskside Labs**, **Liftwork**. Check any name you like in the [USPTO trademark search](https://tmsearch.uspto.gov) and see that the domain is free. Tell me the name you pick and I'll put it in everywhere.

Press **Ctrl+F5** on http://localhost:8080 to see the changes. They aren't committed yet, so your earlier save point is still there if you want to go back. Do you want me to commit this version?

content.text:
You don't have to pick a booking database from scratch: the site already saves bookings to **Google Firestore**, which is free at your size. What's left to decide is whether to keep it and how to track visitors. Here are my recommendations.

### Booking details: keep Firestore (already built)
- **Free tier:** 1 GB of storage and 20,000 saves per day. That's thousands of bookings for $0.
- **Already wired up:** it's Google's own database and works with Cloud Run without passwords or keys, so there's no extra code.
- **Viewing bookings:** you'd read them in the Google Cloud console, which isn't very friendly for daily use. Easy additions:
  - **Copy each booking to a Google Sheet** (also free), so you see new bookings in a spreadsheet.
  - **An email to you for each new booking**, using your Gmail or Resend's free plan (3,000 emails a month).

Other free options and their catches:
- **Supabase:** a free project pauses after a week without use, which is risky for a quiet new site.
- **Google Sheets on its own:** fine at small volume, but it hits limits and is less secure as a database.

### Visitors to the site
One important point first: the site can't legally record *who* each visitor is (names, emails) unless they fill in the form. What you can track freely is **anonymous** activity: how many visits, which pages, which buttons, where visitors came from, and which device they used.
- **Store anonymous visits in Firestore (my recommendation):** a few lines of code. No cookies, so no cookie consent banner, and the data stays in your own Google project. I'd add a simple private stats page showing visits per day, top pages and "Book a call" clicks.
- **Cloudflare Web Analytics:** free, no cookies, with a ready-made dashboard. It needs a free Cloudflare account.
- **Google Analytics 4:** free with the richest reports, but it uses cookies. That means a cookie consent banner for EU/UK visitors, and visitor data goes to Google.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\971367\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\bundled-skills\2.1.295\d6a5b8c2cc3563f9ae6cbfe5e20eefec\dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

input.content:
# Deploys the site to Google Cloud Run with Firestore storage, optional Google Sheet copy,
# optional email alerts, and a password-protected stats page at /admin.
#
# First deploy (example):
#   .\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId my-gcp-project -AdminPassword "a-long-password" `
#     -SheetId 1AbC...xyz -NotifyTo you@gmail.com `
#     -SmtpHost smtp.gmail.com -SmtpPort 587 -SmtpUser you@gmail.com -SmtpPassword "gmail-app-password"
#
# Later deploys: .\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId my-gcp-project
# (passwords are kept in Secret Manager; pass a parameter again only to change it)
#
# Prereqs: gcloud CLI installed, `gcloud auth login` done, billing enabled on the project.
param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$ProjectId,
  [string]$Region = "us-central1",
  [string]$Service = "groundwork-site",
  [string]$FirestoreLocation = "nam5",
  [string]$AdminPassword,
  [string]$SheetId,
  [string]$SheetTab = "Bookings",
  [string]$NotifyTo,
  [string]$NotifyFrom,
  [string]$SmtpHost,
  [string]$SmtpPort = "587",
  [string]$SmtpUser,
  [string]$SmtpPassword
)
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$sa = "$Service-sa@$ProjectId.iam.gserviceaccount.com"

function Test-Secret([string]$Name) {
  $found = gcloud secrets list --filter="name:$Name" --format="value(name)"
  return [bool]$found
}

# Creates the secret if needed and adds a new version. Writes via a temp file so no
# trailing newline sneaks into the value.
function Set-Secret([string]$Name, [string]$Value) {
  if (-not (Test-Secret $Name)) {
    gcloud secrets create $Name --replication-policy=automatic | Out-Null
  }
  $tmp = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName()
  try {
    [System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($tmp, $Value)
    gcloud secrets versions add $Name --data-file=$tmp | Out-Null
  } finally {
    Remove-Item $tmp -Force
  }
  gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding $Name --member="serviceAccount:$sa" --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor" | Out-Null
}

Write-Host "==> Using project $ProjectId"
gcloud config set project $ProjectId

Write-Host "==> Enabling APIs"
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com `
  firestore.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com sheets.googleapis.com

Write-Host "==> Ensuring Firestore (default) database exists"
$dbs = gcloud firestore databases list --format="value(name)" 2>$null
if (-not ($dbs -match "/databases/\(default\)")) {
  gcloud firestore databases create --location=$FirestoreLocation --type=firestore-native
}

Write-Host "==> Auto-deleting daily visitor markers after 2 days (Firestore TTL)"
gcloud firestore fields ttls update expireAt --collection-group=stats_visitors --enable-ttl --async 2>$null | Out-Null

Write-Host "==> Ensuring service account $sa"
$existing = gcloud iam service-accounts list --filter="email:$sa" --format="value(email)"
if (-not $existing) {
  gcloud iam service-accounts create "$Service-sa" --display-name="$Service runtime"
}
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $ProjectId --member="serviceAccount:$sa" --role="roles/datastore.user" --condition=None | Out-Null

Write-Host "==> Secrets"
if ($AdminPassword) { Set-Secret "admin-password" $AdminPassword }
elseif (-not (Test-Secret "admin-password")) { throw "First deploy: pass -AdminPassword so the /admin stats page has a password." }

content.text:
The backend is built the way you chose, and it all runs on free tiers. Bookings and visitor stats work end to end on your computer and all 14 tests pass. The Google Sheet copy and the email alert are written and tested in code, but they haven't sent anything real yet: that needs your Google Cloud project, a Sheet and an email account.

**Booking details:**
1. **Firestore** stays the main record of every booking.
2. **Google Sheet:** each new booking is added as a row. Text is stored exactly as typed and never run as a formula.
3. **Email to you:** each new booking arrives as an email. Hitting Reply goes straight to the visitor. Any email account works; with Gmail you'd use an "app password".

If the Sheet or email fails, the booking is still saved and the problem is only logged.

**Visitors, counted anonymously:**
- **What's counted:** page visits, unique visitors per day, where visitors came from (LinkedIn, Google, typed the address), device type, and clicks on key buttons (each "Book a call" button, the video, the example automations).
- **What isn't stored:** no cookies and no IP addresses, so you don't need a cookie banner. Bots and visitors who've switched on "Do Not Track" aren't counted.

**Your private stats page at `/admin`:** it's password-protected and shows:
- totals for visits, unique visitors, bookings and the share of visitors who booked
- a daily visits chart
- top pages, button clicks, where visitors came from and devices
- your latest 25 bookings

You can switch between 7, 30 and 90 days. In my test it showed 3 visits from 1 visitor, 4 button clicks and the test booking.

**To go live:** run the updated `deploy.ps1` (steps are in the [README](README.md)). It stores your admin and email passwords in Google Secret Manager, never in the code:

```bash
.\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID -AdminPassword "a-long-password" -SheetId YOUR_SHEET_ID -NotifyTo you@gmail.com -SmtpHost smtp.gmail.com -SmtpUser you@gmail.com -SmtpPassword "gmail-app-password"
```

Before running it:
- Create the Google Sheet and add the header row listed in the README.
- After the first deploy, share the Sheet with the service account the script creates (`groundwork-site-sa@…`), give it Editor access, then run the deploy again.

My local test server is running with the temporary password `local-test`. Open http://localhost:8080/admin and enter any username with that password to try it.

# Random string used to make anonymous daily visitor ids. Keep it stable.
-Marketing site and booking form for a hands-on AI setup service aimed at project managers and leaders in
-mechanical, electrical, aviation and marine. Built to run on **Google Cloud Run**, with bookings stored in
-  index.html       Home: hero, About us (click-to-play session animation), Services (live pipeline), Security, How to book
-  book.html        Booking form: name, role, company, industry, email, phone, date/time/time zone, details
-  styles.css       Theme ("engineering drawing": drafting paper, navy ink, safety orange)
-  main.js          Nav, scroll reveals, animation controls
-  server.js        Entry point, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM
-  app.js           Express app: security headers/CSP, rate limiting, API, static files
-  db.js            Storage: Firestore in production, in-memory for local dev
-  notify.js        After a booking: append to Google Sheet + email you (both optional)
-  stats.js         Anonymous visit/click stats helpers (no cookies, no IPs stored)
-  admin/           Private stats page served at /admin (password protected)
-- Strict Content-Security-Policy, HSTS and other headers (helmet). No inline scripts.
-- Rate limiting on bookings (5 per 15 min per IP), 16 KB body limit, honeypot spam trap.
-- Validation runs in the browser and again on the server.
-- Structured JSON logs that show up properly in Cloud Logging.
-- Accessible: skip link, labelled fields, keyboard focus styles, `prefers-reduced-motion` support.
-To try the stats page locally, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, set `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, run `npm run dev`
-## Where the data goes (all free tiers)
-| What | Where | How you see it |

content.text:
Short answers: yes, there's a real backend. GitHub stores your code but doesn't run it. Vercel would need changes. Google Cloud Run works as-is and makes the site public for anyone to use.

### What backend do we have?
The project is a full web app, not just pages. Its server (Node.js) handles:
- **Bookings:** checks the form, blocks spam, saves each booking, and can copy it to a Google Sheet and email you.
- **Visitor stats:** records anonymous page views and clicks.
- **Admin:** the login page and the private `/admin` stats page.
- **Database:** Google Firestore, but only once it's deployed. On your laptop, data is kept in memory and lost when the server stops.

### Upload to GitHub?
Yes, and it's safe: no passwords are in the code. The `.env` file is excluded, and live passwords go into Google Secret Manager. But GitHub only **stores** code. It doesn't run the site, so nobody can visit it from there. GitHub is your backup and version history. I'd use a **private** repo.

### Deploy on Vercel without changes?
Not quite. Vercel can run Express apps like this one, but several things would behave differently:
- **Database access:** on Google Cloud the app connects to Firestore automatically. On Vercel you'd have to create a Google key file and store it in Vercel's settings, which is extra work and a security risk to manage.
- **Spam and login limits:** Vercel runs many short-lived copies of the app, so the "5 bookings per 15 minutes" and "10 wrong passwords" limits wouldn't hold reliably.
- **Security headers:** Vercel serves the pages directly, skipping the server's security headers unless they're copied into a Vercel config file.

So it's possible, but it needs rework and it's less secure.

### Deploy so others can access it?
Yes. **Google Cloud Run** is what this project was built for:
1. Install the Google Cloud CLI and log in.
2. Create a Google Cloud project and turn on billing. A card is required, but this site should normally stay within the free tier, so $0.
3. Run `deploy.ps1`.

You get a public `https://…run.app` address that anyone can open on a phone or laptop, and it runs all the time. You can connect your own domain later.

Before sharing it publicly:
- Replace the **Groundwork AI** name, which is already used by other companies.
- Replace the placeholder email `hello@example.com`.
- Add a **privacy policy** page, because you collect names, emails and phone numbers.

**My recommendation:** GitHub (private) for the code, plus Cloud Run for the live site. Cloud Run can also redeploy automatically every time you push to GitHub.

The latest changes (backend, stats and login page) aren't committed yet. Do you want me to commit them and create a private GitHub repo? Creating the repo and pushing means uploading your code to GitHub, so I'll only do that once you say yes.

content.text:
These steps are for your Windows laptop. Expect about 30–45 minutes the first time.

**Before you start:** use a **personal Google account** (for example Gmail) for this business, not your Cognizant work account. If your work laptop blocks installing software, do this on a personal computer: copy over the `ai-service-site` folder, without `node_modules`, and also install Node.js (version 20 or later) and run `npm install` in that folder.

---

### Step 1: Install the Google Cloud CLI
1. Open PowerShell and run:
   ```bash
   winget install Google.CloudSDK
   ```
   If `winget` doesn't work, download the installer from https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install (Windows tab) and run it with the default options.
2. **Close and reopen** PowerShell, then check it's installed:
   ```bash
   gcloud --version
   ```

### Step 2: Log in
```bash
gcloud auth login
```
A browser window opens. Sign in with your personal Google account and click **Allow**.

### Step 3: Create a Google Cloud project
1. Go to https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate
2. Enter a project name, e.g. `ai-service-site`.
3. Under the name, Google shows a **Project ID**, e.g. `ai-service-site-473812`. Copy it: you'll need it in every command below.
4. Click **Create**.

### Step 4: Turn on billing and set a spending alert
1. Go to https://console.cloud.google.com/billing and make sure your new project is selected at the top.
2. Click **Link a billing account**, then **Create billing account**, and enter your card details. A small site like this should normally cost $0; billing just has to be on for Cloud Run to work.
3. **Set a budget alert** (strongly recommended). In Billing, open **Budgets & alerts**, click **Create budget**, set the amount to **$5** and keep the email alerts on. If costs ever start, you'll get an email.

### Step 5 (optional): Prepare the Google Sheet and email alerts
Skip this if you only want bookings on the `/admin` page. You can add these later.

**Google Sheet:**
1. Create a new Google Sheet and rename the first tab to **Bookings**.
2. In row 1, put these headers, one per column:
   `Received (UTC)`, `Reference`, `Name`, `Role`, `Company`, `Industry`, `Email`, `Phone`, `Preferred date`, `Preferred time`, `Time zone`, `Other availability`, `Details`
3. Copy the Sheet ID from its web address: `docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/`**`THIS-PART`**`/edit`

**Email alerts (Gmail):**
1. Go to https://myaccount.google.com/security and turn on **2-Step Verification** if it's off.
2. Go to https://myaccount.google.com/apppasswords, create an app password named "website", and copy the 16-character password.

### Step 6: Deploy
1. Open PowerShell in the project folder:
   ```bash
   cd C:\Users\971367\ai-service-site
   ```
2. Allow the deploy script to run in this window only (Windows blocks scripts by default):
   ```bash
   Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
   ```
3. Run the deploy, replacing the capitalised values with your own.

   **With Sheet and email:**
   ```bash
   .\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID -AdminPassword "CHOOSE-A-LONG-PASSWORD" -SheetId YOUR_SHEET_ID -NotifyTo you@gmail.com -SmtpHost smtp.gmail.com -SmtpUser you@gmail.com -SmtpPassword "YOUR-16-CHAR-APP-PASSWORD"
   ```
   **Or the simplest version** (bookings only on `/admin`):
   ```bash
   .\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID -AdminPassword "CHOOSE-A-LONG-PASSWORD"
   ```
4. If it asks *"create an Artifact Registry repository?"*, type **Y**.
5. Wait about 3–5 minutes. At the end it prints:
   ```
   Site:  https://groundwork-site-xxxxx.us-central1.run.app
   Stats: https://groundwork-site-xxxxx.us-central1.run.app/admin
   ```
   That **Site** address is your live website, and anyone can open it.

### Step 7 (only if you did Step 5): Give the site access to your Sheet
1. Open your Google Sheet and click **Share**.
2. Add `groundwork-site-sa@YOUR_PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com` (the deploy creates this account), set it to **Editor**, untick "Notify people", and click **Share**.

You don't need to deploy again for this: once shared, new bookings start appearing in the Sheet.

### Step 8: Test it
1. Open the **Site** address on your phone and laptop.
2. Make a test booking.
3. Check that:
   - it appears at **/admin** (log in with your admin password)
   - a new row appears in the **Sheet**
   - you get an **email**
4. Delete the test booking afterwards: Google Cloud Console → **Firestore** → `bookings`.

---

### Later
- **After you change the website,** run `.\deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID` again (after Step 6's `Set-ExecutionPolicy` line). Your passwords and settings are kept.
- **To change the admin password,** run the same command with `-AdminPassword "new-password"` added.
- **To use your own domain** (e.g. yourbusiness.com), buy it from a domain seller, then in Cloud Console go to **Cloud Run** → your service → **Manage custom domains** and follow the steps.
- **If anything fails,** copy the full error message from PowerShell and paste it here, and I'll tell you how to fix it.

Before sharing the link widely, remember to:
- change the brand name

message.content: Instead of using SDK, can I login to cloud online, and upload the project directly, or first upload to git and then to the GCP?

content.text:
Yes, both work, and you don't need to install anything on your laptop for either. One limit: you can't upload a project folder straight into Cloud Run's website. It deploys either from a GitHub repository or from a terminal. There are two browser-only routes:

---

## Option A: Google Cloud Shell (quickest, ~15 minutes)
Cloud Shell is a free terminal that runs inside the Google Cloud website and already has all the Google tools installed. You upload the project and run the same deploy script there.

1. **Zip the project.** In File Explorer, open `C:\Users\971367\ai-service-site`, select everything **except** the `node_modules` folder, right-click → **Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder**, and name it `site.zip`. Google installs the libraries itself when it builds the site.
2. Go to https://console.cloud.google.com, create the project, and link billing. These are the same as Steps 3–4 in my previous message.
3. Click the **Cloud Shell** icon (**>_**) at the top right. A terminal opens at the bottom of the page.
4. In the Cloud Shell toolbar, click **⋮ (More) → Upload** and choose `site.zip`.
5. In the terminal, type:
   ```bash
   mkdir site && cd site && unzip ../site.zip
   ```
   ```bash
   pwsh ./deploy.ps1 -ProjectId YOUR_PROJECT_ID -AdminPassword "CHOOSE-A-LONG-PASSWORD"
   ```
   Add the Sheet and email options from before if you want them. Cloud Shell includes PowerShell (`pwsh`), so the same script works. If `pwsh` isn't found, tell me and I'll give you a Linux version of the script.
6. It prints your public **Site** address when it's done.

**Downside:** to publish later changes, you have to upload a new zip and run the script again.

---

## Option B: GitHub, then automatic deploys to Cloud Run (best long-term)
Your code lives in a private GitHub repo. Cloud Run watches it, and **every time you push a change, the live site updates by itself.** Everything is done by clicking in the Google Cloud website. Setup takes longer (~30 minutes), because the jobs `deploy.ps1` did for you are now done by hand, once.

**1. Put the code on GitHub** as a private repo. I can do this for you.

**2. In the Google Cloud website, one-time setup:**
1. **Create the database:** go to **Firestore → Create database**, choose **Native mode**, keep the ID `(default)`, set Location to **nam5**, and click **Create**.
2. **Create the service account** (the identity the site runs as): go to **IAM & Admin → Service accounts → Create**, name it `groundwork-site-sa`, give it the role **Cloud Datastore User**, and click **Done**.
3. **Store the passwords:** go to **Secret Manager → Create secret** and make these three:
   - `admin-password`: your admin password
   - `stats-salt`: any long random text, e.g. mash the keyboard for 30 characters
   - `smtp-password`: your Gmail app password. Only needed if you want email alerts.

   For each secret, open it → **Permissions → Grant access**, enter `groundwork-site-sa@YOUR_PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, and give it the role **Secret Manager Secret Accessor**.
4. **Auto-delete old visitor records (optional):** go to **Firestore → Time-to-live → Create policy**, with collection group `stats_visitors` and timestamp field `expireAt`.

**3. Create the Cloud Run service:**
1. Go to **Cloud Run → Deploy container → Service** and choose **Continuously deploy from a repository**.
2. Click **Set up with Cloud Build** and connect GitHub: authorize it, pick your repo, branch `main`, Build type **Dockerfile**.
3. Set Service name `groundwork-site` and Region `us-central1`.
4. Under **Authentication**, choose **Allow public access**.
5. Open **Containers, Volumes, Networking, Security**:
   - **Variables & Secrets** tab:
     - Environment variables: `STORAGE` = `firestore` and `FIRESTORE_COLLECTION` = `bookings`.
       For Sheet and email, also add `SHEET_ID`, `NOTIFY_TO`, `SMTP_HOST` = `smtp.gmail.com`, `SMTP_PORT` = `587` and `SMTP_USER`.
     - **Reference a secret:** `ADMIN_PASSWORD` → `admin-password` (latest), `STATS_SALT` → `stats-salt` (latest), and `SMTP_PASS` → `smtp-password` (latest).
   - **Security** tab: set Service account to `groundwork-site-sa`.
6. Click **Create**. After a few minutes, the public web address appears at the top of the page.

From then on, every push to GitHub redeploys the site automatically.

---

**My recommendation:** **Option B** if you'll keep changing the site, which you probably will (new name, privacy page, wording). Use **Option A** if you just want it live today.
